lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7, what are work songs? (Songs sung to keep a steady beat while people work together.) Today: how music shows who we are: our cultures and our communities.
Every culture makes music for the moments that matter: lullabies, weddings, festivals, sport and remembering. Music says: this is us, and this is how we celebrate.
Many styles grew in one place, then spread: tango in Argentina and Uruguay, flamenco in Spain, fado in Portugal, reggae in Jamaica, samba in Brazil and gamelan in Indonesia.
In West Africa, griots are musicians and storytellers who keep their people's history in song. Many play the kora, a harp with 21 strings.
Music travels with people: when people moved, they brought their songs, and new styles grew where they met. Reggae grew in Jamaica in the 1960s, and Bob Marley (1945-1981) took it round the world.
Music changes how we feel. Slow, soft music with a steady beat helps many people calm down; a shared song can make a whole crowd feel as one. Listen to a gentle lullaby.
Worked example: festivals have their own music. Carnival in Trinidad has drums and steelpans; Diwali has songs and lamps. Christmas has carols, and the Lunar New Year has lion dances with drums.
Try it in the world: ask a grown-up which song reminds them of home, and listen together. In LIFE, the Calm Corner has ways to feel calm; music can be one. Next: big musical forms.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Which moment is this music best for?
exercises.hint: Is it slow and soft, or loud and strong?
exercises.explain: It is slow, soft and gentle, with a rocking feel: a lullaby.

exercises.prompt: Match each style to where it grew.
exercises.hint: Think of the lesson's list of places.
exercises.explain: Tango grew in Argentina and Uruguay, flamenco in Spain, reggae in Jamaica, samba in Brazil and gamelan in Indonesia.

exercises.prompt: A griot is a West African musician who keeps history in song.
exercises.explain: True: griots are musicians and storytellers who keep their people's history.

exercises.prompt: Copy this rhythm from Cuban music: part of the clave.
exercises.hint: Count the boxes between the claps.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Which moment is this music best for?
exercises.hint: Is the beat strong and steady?
exercises.explain: A strong, steady beat and bright notes: music to march to in a parade.

exercises.prompt: Listen. What sounds under the tune all the time?
choices: a drone: one low note held
exercises.hint: Listen below the tune: does something stay the same?
exercises.explain: One low note is held under the whole tune: a drone, as bagpipes and many folk musics use.

exercises.prompt: Does it help people feel calm, or excite them?
exercises.hint: Imagine it at bedtime, then at a match.
exercises.explain: Slow, soft music with a gentle beat and lullabies calm; loud drums and chanting excite.

exercises.prompt: The kora is a West African harp with 21 strings.
exercises.explain: True: the kora has 21 strings and is played by griots.

exercises.prompt: Bob Marley was born in 1945. How old was he at the end of 1970?
Why do crowds at a match sing together?
choices: a shared song makes them feel as one
exercises.hint: Think of how singing together feels.
exercises.explain: Singing the same song together makes a crowd feel like one team: music builds community.

exercises.prompt: Listen. How many different notes does this tune use?
exercises.hint: Listen for the notes again and again.
exercises.explain: It uses only C, D, E, G and A: 5 notes, the pentatonic scale many folk tunes use.

exercises.hint: Listen for where the claps come in pairs.
exercises.explain: Claps in boxes 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7: one clap, then two pairs of quicker claps, as samba drums play.

exercises.prompt: Listen: the drone stays on one note all the way through.
exercises.hint: Listen to the low part only.
exercises.explain: True: the low A holds on under the whole tune while the melody moves above it, A, B, C sharp, E and back, like the drone of bagpipes.

exercises.prompt: Match each moment to music that suits it.
exercises.hint: Think of the feeling each moment needs.
exercises.explain: Weddings have dances, bedtime a lullaby, remembering a slow song and a match chants and drums.

exercises.prompt: A song reminds someone of their grandparents' home. What does this show?
exercises.hint: Why can one song bring back a place?
exercises.explain: A song heard again and again in one place, with one family, holds memories of them. Hearing it brings them back, so music becomes part of who we are.

exercises.prompt: A gamelan piece goes round in cycles of 16 beats, and a big gong ends each cycle. How many gong strokes in 64 beats?
exercises.hint: How many cycles of 16 fit in 64?
exercises.explain: Each cycle is 16 beats and ends with one gong stroke. 64 ÷ 16 = 4 cycles, so the gong sounds 4 times.
